name: Insurance-Float Capture: Permanent Capital for Private Investments
deck: Alternative asset managers embed insurance subsidiaries to access premium float as permanent capital funding higher-fee private investments. KKR, Apollo, Brookfield, Berkshire, and MetLife operate insurance platforms converting policyholder premiums into permanent deployment capital.
core_bet: Insurance float—premiums collected today for claims paid in the future—becomes the most durable form of permanent capital for alternative managers. Apollo is the purest live example: its Athene retirement-services arm generated $3.4B of spread-related earnings in FY2025, larger than its $2.5B of classic fee-related earnings, proving the balance-sheet engine now outweighs the fund-management engine. By owning insurance, managers gain captive funding that is cheaper than raised-fund capital and deployable into private credit they originate themselves.

mechanism: Insurance subsidiaries provide permanent balance-sheet capital divorced from fund-raise cycles. KKR's insurance relationship and Apollo/Brookfield's insurance platforms access policyholder premiums that are available immediately and do not depend on institutional fundraising success. Unlike raised capital that has redemption dates and return expectations, insurance float is permanent and can be deployed into illiquid private investments with decades-long holds.

Fee stacking amplifies returns through alternative-manager economics. When private capital managers deploy insurance float into their own private equity, credit, or infrastructure funds, they capture management fees (typically 2% annually) plus carried interest (typically 20% of profits). Insurance float is cheaper than retail capital because insurance regulators focus on claims coverage, not absolute returns; this allows alternative managers to invest insurance float into higher-risk or lower-return-profile assets that would not meet external capital expectations.

Insurance integration becomes a balance-sheet and capital-structure arbitrage. Berkshire Hathaway has been the masterclass in this model for decades: insurance underwriting generates float (liabilities) that Berkshire invests into wholly-owned businesses and long-dated securities. KKR, Apollo, and Brookfield are replicating this pattern: acquire insurance operations, use the float for permanent capital deployment, and capture both the insurance margin and the investment return.
why_now: Through 2025-2026, insurance-float colonization accelerates because: (1) alternative managers have accumulated so much capital that fundraising becomes inefficient, (2) institutional investors are increasingly skeptical of new fund commitments at higher fees, (3) insurance float provides a 'second balance sheet' that circumvents fundraising limits, (4) the insurance underwriting margin is attractive in its own right, and (5) scale matters—only the largest alternative managers can afford to acquire meaningful insurance platforms. KKR's record FRE and 'strongest monetization quarter ever' reflect the combined economics of insurance operations plus private-markets deployment.
who_pays: Insurance policyholders funding premiums that become permanent capital for alternative managers; pension funds and endowments who could have purchased directly but instead provide capital to alternative managers who deploy to insurance-backed strategies; retail insurance customers whose premiums subsidize lower-fee deployment of capital.
who_profits: KKR, Apollo, Brookfield, Berkshire, MetLife, and other large alternative managers or conglomerates that own meaningful insurance platforms. They capture insurance underwriting margins (typically 2-5% net margins), management fees on deployed capital (2% AUM), and carried interest on profits (20%). The compounding creates a dual profit pool: one from insurance operations, one from alternative-asset management.
tension: The model breaks if: (1) insurance regulators begin restricting how much capital can be invested in illiquid alternatives, (2) insurance underwriting deteriorates and float shrinks due to claim losses, (3) deployed returns on insurance float disappoint, lowering the appeal of the balance-sheet arbitrage, or (4) new competitors enter and bid up acquisition prices for insurance platforms, making the economics uncompetitive. Regulatory scrutiny of alternative managers using insurance float for risky deployments remains a live risk.
surprising_part: The insurance-float model is not new—Berkshire perfected it decades ago. The surprise is that alternative-asset managers like KKR and Apollo are only now systematically acquiring insurance platforms at scale. This reflects a shift: when private-markets capital becomes abundant enough, alternative managers recognize that insurance float is cheaper than institutional fundraising and that the regulatory arbitrage (insurance regulators are less demanding than asset-management regulators) makes the economics compelling.
one_sentence: Alternative managers are building insurance subsidiaries to access permanent capital (policyholder premiums) and deploy it into higher-fee private investments, creating a parallel profit stream from underwriting.
societal_stake: When insurance float becomes a financing mechanism for alternative-asset managers' private investments, insurance policyholders are indirectly funding those strategies without knowing it. If those private investments underperform, insurance float could be eroded, raising costs for policyholders or threatening claims payments. The model also concentrates capital-deployment power: only the largest alternative managers can afford to acquire insurance platforms, potentially limiting competition and capital access for smaller managers.

evidence.fact: FY2025 spread-related earnings through Athene were about $3.4B, exceeding the ~$2.5B of fee-related earnings — the insurance-float engine is now larger than the fund-management engine. The packet describes the model explicitly as 'management fees plus spread earnings through Athene, backed by origination, retirement services, and insurance-scale balance-sheet sourcing.'

Record origination of more than $300B in FY2025 and total AUM of about $938B (rising to ~$1.05T by 2Q26); Apollo is described as 'a bridge between alternative asset management and balance-sheet-intensive financial intermediation,' manufacturing investment-grade and private credit at scale into insurance and retirement channels.

The original float model: FY2025 insurance underwriting earnings of $7.258B plus insurance investment income of $12.513B — Berkshire generates its float at a profit and then earns investment income on top. The packet calls it 'a conglomerate that uses insurance float... to keep reallocating capital across the portfolio.'

A pure-play liability-and-asset system: 2Q26 net investment income of about $6.7B on premiums/fees/other revenues of about $13.7B, with a new $3.0B buyback authorization (Aug 2026); FY2025 returned nearly $4.4B to shareholders. Described as 'a global liability-and-asset management system' rather than a simple insurer.
Total AUM grew to about $796B (2Q26) from $744B at FY2025 year-end, deploying a permanent-capital base alongside its Global Atlantic insurance relationship.

In 2Q26 alone, spread-related earnings of about $877M nearly matched fee-related earnings of about $785M, showing the insurance-float profit stream is a co-equal driver quarter to quarter, not a supplement.
